description:
FILED s470bp (Opus, 2026-09-05), measured while #1188 shipped the module-fasl
cache.  THIS IS THE SECOND HALF OF THE MODULE-LOAD CONSTANT and, after #1188,
the biggest single number left in the yardstick (plan-speed-and-ir-s470 §A.4.1).

THE MEASUREMENT.  With the module fasl cache on and every module hot,
`pcl -E 'use JSON::PP; print 1'` still takes 1.43 s (perl 0.0098 s), and
PCL_FASL_DEBUG shows where: the JSON::PP module load itself is

    PCL: module PP.pm -> FASL HIT (0.858s)

with Exporter/Boolean/Carp/Scalar::Util at 0.001 s each.  So 0.86 s is spent
INSIDE a fasl load that compiles nothing of its own.  sb-sprof over the same
program (scratch/s470bp/json-graph.prof) attributes the frames under it to
`sb-c::ir1-convert` / `ir1-optimize` — the SBCL COMPILER — reached from
`pcl:p-eval` and `eval`.

THE CAUSE, in JSON::PP's own source (5.40.3, lib/5.40.3/JSON/PP.pm:79-99):

    for my $name (@xs_compati_bit_properties, @pp_bit_properties) {
        my $property_id = 'P_' . uc($name);
        eval qq/ sub $name { ... } sub get_$name { ... } /;
    }

~20 string `eval`s at module load, each generating two subs.  Every one is a
`pl2cl --server` round trip plus an SBCL compile of the result, EVERY RUN — the
`eval "1"` constant (0.29 s cold / ~40 ms warm-server) multiplied by the number
of generated subs.  It is not JSON::PP-specific: generate-accessors-with-eval is
the standard pure-Perl idiom (Class::Accessor, Moo/Sub::Quote's quote_sub,
Moose, Type::Tiny), so it is on the load path of most OO CPAN code.

THE DESIGN, and it is the #1188 mechanism reused, not a new one.  `p-eval`
already has an in-PROCESS cache keyed by the eval TEXT plus the capture NAMES
(#296-B1: the alist's VALUES resolve at run time, so the compiled code is
reusable for any values).  That key is therefore process-independent, and the
same three ingredients #1188 uses make it a DISK key:

    <sxhash of (perl text, package, capture names, features)>
      + *pcl-cache-generation* + *pcl-runtime-identity*      -> .lisp / .fasl

On a miss: transpile (as now), write the text, compile-file it with
*PCL-FASL-BUILD* bound (an eval body has the same BEGIN/sub-install ordering
question a module does), load the fasl, funcall the thunk.  On a hit: load the
fasl and funcall.  Failure falls back to today's path exactly as the module
cache does; a `.failed` marker stops a doomed compile being re-paid.

WHAT TO CHECK BEFORE BUILDING IT (each is a real question, not a formality):
  * the ONE key.  Read `p-eval`'s existing cache key first and extend THAT
    (rule 11) — a second spelling of "what makes two evals the same" is how the
    capture-alist rule (#296-B1, #387) would drift.
  * an eval's thunk closes over its CALLER's lexicals through the alist.  A
    fasl can only hold code, so the thunk must take the alist as an ARGUMENT,
    which is what the in-process cache already relies on — verify, do not
    assume.
  * `eval` inside a sub inside a loop: the same text at the same site with
    different capture VALUES must hit the cache (probe: two subs, same eval
    text, expect the #296-B1 "ABA" answer, which s418c already probed).
  * an eval whose text is built at run time and never repeats is a pure LOSS
    (one extra compile-file + a cache file).  Measure the hit rate over the
    board before enabling it unconditionally; a size/count cap may be needed.
  * $@ / die inside the eval must behave identically — the eval's error path is
    perl-visible, unlike a module load's.

BAR when taken: the gate, the full sweep (module and eval loads are invisible
to corpus-diff), the CPAN board (this is exactly what it exercises), and these
constants re-measured on a quiet box:

    use JSON::PP; print 1     1.432 s  (#1188's number; target ~0.3 s)
    use Moo; print 1          0.417 s
    eval "1"; print 1         ~0.29 s


=== DONE (s473p, 2026-09-07) — the TRANSPILE half; the fasl half is #1410 ===
SHIPPED as `59f2214b`.  A string eval's emission is now cached on DISK under
<cache>/evals/<md5>.lisp with a .deps sidecar beside it, so the pl2cl round
trip is paid once EVER instead of once per run.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT CHOSE THE DESIGN (scratch/s473p/probe1.lisp, on the PCL
core, one eval-shaped CL text):
    pl2cl --server round trip   ~16 ms   (= 0.710 s for 20 DISTINCT evals of
                                          this shape vs 0.404 s for 20
                                          IDENTICAL ones, startup subtracted)
    READ + EVAL of the CL text    5.00 ms
    COMPILE-FILE of the same     10.00 ms
    loading the resulting fasl     0.05 ms
So the TRANSPILE is three quarters of an eval's cost and it is the three
quarters a cache can take with no semantic question at all: the string that
comes back is the same string.  The fasl quarter is NOT taken here — see #1410.

THE POPULATION, measured with a temporary counter in p-eval:
  * `use JSON::PP; print 1` runs **80** string evals (not the ~20 this task
    guessed), and the same 80 keys arrive in the same order on every run;
  * three eval-heavy perl-tests files (eval.t, signatures.t, method.t) run 842
    evals of which 652 are DISTINCT — so a run-once eval is the normal case
    there and the cache directory had to join the 30-day prune.

THE FIVE PRE-CHECKS THIS TASK ASKED FOR, each answered:
  * THE ONE KEY: p-eval's existing in-process cache-key (perl TEXT, perl
    package, capture NAMES, features) IS the disk key, plus
    *pcl-cache-generation* — the same ingredient a module's cache path carries.
    Hashed with MD5, not sxhash: a run reaches dozens of module paths and
    thousands of eval texts, and a collision would run one eval's code for
    another's.
  * THE ALIST IS AN ARGUMENT, verified not assumed: the thunk resolves free
    names at RUN time through p-eval-lex-lookup, so the cached text is reusable
    for any values — probed with two subs sharing one eval text (#296-B1's
    "ABA", and it is a guard row).
  * SAME TEXT, TWO PACKAGES: two entries, because pkg-name is in the key
    (guard row: P1/P2).
  * A FAILING COMPILE IS NOT CACHED — p-transpile-string signals, so no .lisp
    and no .deps is written, and the next run pays the same failure, as perl
    recompiles every time (guard rows + a probe: `eval "my $q = ;"` twice).
  * A NEVER-REPEATED EVAL is a near-zero loss: one small file write (~0.1 ms),
    NOT a compile.  That is the reason the fasl half is a separate task.

VALIDITY is the module cache's minus the clause an eval has no subject for.
There is no source FILE to be newer than, so what remains is the #1261
dependency manifest — needed, because an eval whose text `use`s a module reads
that module's prototypes.  `pl2cl --server`'s request gained a deps-path line
and writes the sidecar BEFORE it answers; a .lisp whose .deps is missing or
stale is a MISS (p-cm-valid-p defaults to NIL), which makes "deps first, .lisp
second" the whole publication rule.  ONE reader: %p-read-manifest is now a
caller of the new %p-manifest-at, which takes the path.  Verified live: an
eval that `use`s a module records its md5, and touching the module
re-transpiles the entry.

MEASURED, interleaved A/B against b5e9f845 on a quiet box (load 1.1-1.3),
best-of-7, startup as the byte-identical control:
    print 1                (control)  0.170 -> 0.169   0.99x
    eval "1"; print 1                 0.304 -> 0.172   0.57x
    use Moo; print 1                  0.343 -> 0.201   0.59x
    use JSON::PP; print 1             1.129 -> 0.409   0.36x
The task's acceptance target was "~0.3 s" for JSON::PP; 0.409 s is what the
transpile half alone reaches, and the eval-"1" constant is now startup + 3 ms
(the pl2cl server is never spawned on an all-hit run).
Absolute, interleaved, best-of-5: json-rt N=100 2.619 -> 1.954 (-25 %),
N=200 4.208 -> 3.533 (-16 %), per-iteration slope unchanged (1.589 -> 1.579),
i.e. the whole move is the constant; moo-objs N=0 4.222 -> 3.840, N=20000
6.144 -> 5.619.

A MEASUREMENT TRAP WORTH RECORDING: `tools/bench-exec.pl` reports moo-objs and
json-rt as REGRESSIONS for a structural reason — its t(N) - t(0) cancels the
constant, and this change makes t(0) smaller, so the win is subtracted away and
what is left is noise.  Absolute interleaved numbers are the honest ones here,
and absolute seconds are the metric (plan §A.0).

BARS: gate 217 files / 7541 rows (only the 13 pclxs xs rows); corpus-diff
IDENTICAL over 111 + 6 shapes, silent drops 5; emission-ab 25 lib files SAME=25
DIFF=0 RCDIFF=0 (no emission change, so no generation bump); FULL SWEEP GATE
clean, 0 new / 0 fixed / 0 LOST, TOTAL passing 18674 (+0), drops 5 = census;
ir-conform 289 pass / 0 fail / 56 known / 0 stale.  NOTE: the sweep and every
other test runner set *pcl-skip-cache*, so the sweep proves the UNCACHED path
is untouched; the cached path is covered by twelve probes vs perl 5.40.3 (cold
run == warm run == --no-cache == PCL_NO_CACHE, byte for byte) and by a 70-file
cpan-tests population run of ./pcl twice against a fresh cache directory: 70
SAME / 0 DIFF.  Guard Pl/t/eval-cache-01.t (16 rows, 8 s), inverse-verified on
a b5e9f845 extraction (rows 4, 13, 14, 16 fail there).
subject: A string eval is COMPILED EVERY RUN: after #1188 the residue of `use JSON::PP` is 0.86 s of `p-eval`, ~20 evals JSON::PP runs at load — the eval cache needs to reach DISK, keyed like the module cache
